fields.title: Power Through Prayer
fields.subtitle: Men Are God's Method
fields.description: E. M. Bounds wrote for preachers, and his argument is single: the Church is looking for better methods, but God is looking for better men. In twenty short chapters, each opening with the words of an earlier praying man, he presses the case that a sermon's power is made in the closet before it is made in the study, and that unction — which no learning, genius or eloquence can win — is bought with much prayer or not at all. Bracing, and hard to read comfortably.

fields.title: Men of Prayer Needed
fields.body_html:
Make holiness of life in every part your study. All your usefulness depends on it, for your sermons last only an hour or two, but your life preaches all week long. If Satan can only turn a covetous minister into a lover of praise, of pleasure, of good food, he has ruined your ministry. Give yourself to prayer, and get your texts, your thoughts and your words from God. Luther spent his best three hours in prayer.—Robert Murray McCheyne

We are constantly stretching, if not straining, to come up with new methods, new plans and new organizations to advance the Church and to make the gospel spread further and work better. This tendency of our day easily loses sight of the man, or buries the man inside the plan or the organization. God’s plan is to make much of the man — far more of him than of anything else. Men are God’s method. The Church is looking for better methods; God is looking for better men. “There was a man sent from God whose name was John.” The whole dispensation that announced Christ and prepared His way was bound up in that one man, John. “Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given.” The world’s salvation comes out of that Son in the cradle. When Paul points to the personal character of the men who planted the gospel in the world, he explains the mystery of their success. The glory and the power of the gospel are staked on the men who proclaim it. When God declares that “the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him,” He is declaring that men are necessary, and that He depends on them as the channel through which to exert His power on the world. This vital, urgent truth is one that our age of machinery is likely to forget. Forgetting it does as much harm to the work of God as knocking the sun out of its place in the sky would do to the world. Darkness, confusion and death would follow.

What the Church needs today is not more machinery, or better machinery, not new organizations or more and newer methods, but men whom the Holy Ghost can use — men of prayer, men mighty in prayer. The Holy Ghost does not flow through methods, but through men. He does not come on machinery, but on men. He does not anoint plans, but men — men of prayer.

A distinguished historian once said that the accidents of personal character have more to do with the revolutions of nations than either philosophical historians or democratic politicians will admit. This truth applies fully to the gospel of Christ: it is the character and conduct of Christ’s followers that Christianize the world and transform nations and individuals. And of the preachers of the gospel it is supremely true.

The character of the gospel, as well as its fortunes, is entrusted to the preacher. He makes or spoils God’s message to people. The preacher is the golden pipe through which the divine oil flows. The pipe must not only be golden; it must be open and without a flaw, so that the oil can flow fully, freely and without any waste.

The man makes the preacher. God must make the man. The messenger is, if anything, more than the message. The preacher is more than the sermon. The preacher makes the sermon. Just as the life-giving milk from a mother’s breast is nothing but the mother’s own life, so everything the preacher says is colored and soaked through by what the preacher is. The treasure is in earthen vessels, and the taste of the vessel seeps into it and may discolor it. The man — the whole man — stands behind the sermon. Preaching is not the performance of an hour. It is the outflow of a life. It takes twenty years to make a sermon, because it takes twenty years to make the man. The true sermon is a living thing. The sermon grows because the man grows. The sermon is forceful because the man is forceful. The sermon is holy because the man is holy. The sermon is full of the divine unction because the man is full of the divine unction.

Paul called it “My gospel.” He did not mean that he had cheapened it with his personal quirks or diverted it by selfishly claiming it. He meant that the gospel had been put into the heart and lifeblood of the man Paul, as a personal trust to be carried out through his own Pauline traits, set on fire and empowered by the fiery energy of his fiery soul. Paul’s sermons — what were they? Where are they? Skeletons and scattered fragments, floating on the sea of inspiration! But the man Paul, greater than his sermons, lives forever, in full form, feature and stature, with his shaping hand still on the Church. The preaching is only a voice. The voice dies into silence, the text is forgotten, the sermon fades from memory; the preacher lives on.

The sermon cannot rise higher in its life-giving power than the man who preaches it. Dead men produce dead sermons, and dead sermons kill. Everything depends on the spiritual character of the preacher. Under the Jewish dispensation the high priest wore a golden plate on his forehead, inscribed in jeweled letters: “Holiness to the Lord.” In the same way, every preacher in Christ’s ministry must be shaped by this same holy motto and governed by it. It is a crying shame for the Christian ministry to fall lower than the Jewish priesthood in holiness of character and holiness of purpose. Jonathan Edwards said: “I went on with my eager pursuit of more holiness and conformity to Christ. The heaven I desired was a heaven of holiness.” The gospel of Christ does not advance on waves of popularity. It has no power to spread itself. It moves as the men who are in charge of it move. The preacher must embody the gospel in his own person. Its divine and most distinctive features must be lived out in him. The constraining power of love must be in the preacher as a driving, unconventional, all-commanding force that forgets itself. The energy of self-denial must be his very being — his heart and blood and bones. He must go out as a man among men, clothed with humility, living in meekness, wise as a serpent, harmless as a dove; wearing the chains of a servant with the spirit of a king — a king in his high, royal, independent bearing, yet with the simplicity and sweetness of a child. The preacher must throw himself into his work for the salvation of people with all the abandon of a perfect, self-emptying faith and a self-consuming zeal. The men who take hold of a generation and shape it for God must be wholehearted, heroic, compassionate, fearless martyrs. If they are timid time-servers or position-seekers, if they are people-pleasers or afraid of people, if their faith has only a weak hold on God or His Word, if their self-denial is broken by any form of self or the world, they cannot take hold of either the Church or the world for God.

The preacher’s sharpest and strongest preaching should be to himself. His hardest, most delicate, most laborious and most thorough work must be done on himself. Training the twelve was the great, difficult and lasting work of Christ. Preachers are not sermon-makers but man-makers and saint-makers, and the only one well trained for this business is the one who has made himself a man and a saint. What God needs is not great talents, or great learning, or great preachers, but men great in holiness, great in faith, great in love, great in faithfulness, great for God — men who are always preaching, by holy sermons in the pulpit and by holy lives out of it. Men like these can shape a generation for God.

This is the pattern on which the early Christians were formed. They were men of solid make, preachers of the heavenly type — heroic, sturdy, soldierly, saintly. For them, preaching meant self-denying, self-crucifying, serious, toilsome, martyr’s work. They gave themselves to it in a way that left its mark on their generation and formed within it a generation yet unborn for God. The preaching man must be the praying man. Prayer is the preacher’s mightiest weapon. It is an almighty force in itself, and it gives life and force to everything else.

The real sermon is made in the prayer closet. The man — God’s man — is made in the prayer closet. His life and his deepest convictions were born in his secret communion with God. The burdened, tearful agony of his spirit, and his weightiest and sweetest messages, came to him when he was alone with God. Prayer makes the man; prayer makes the preacher; prayer makes the pastor.

The pulpit of our day is weak in praying. The pride of learning works against the dependent humility of prayer. Too often prayer in the pulpit is merely official — a performance that is part of the routine of the service. To the modern pulpit, prayer is not the mighty force it was in Paul’s life and Paul’s ministry. Every preacher who does not make prayer a mighty factor in his own life and ministry is a weak factor in God’s work and has no power to advance God’s cause in this world.

fields.title: Our Sufficiency Is of God
fields.body_html:
But above all he excelled in prayer. The inwardness and weight of his spirit, the reverence and solemnity of his speech and manner, and the fewness and fullness of his words often struck even strangers with admiration, just as they used to bring comfort to others. The most awe-filled, living, reverent spirit I ever felt or saw, I must say, was in his prayer. And truly it was a testimony. He knew the Lord and lived nearer to Him than other men, for those who know Him best will see the most reason to approach Him with reverence and fear.—William Penn, of George Fox

The sweetest graces, only slightly twisted, can bear the bitterest fruit. The sun gives life, but sunstroke is death. Preaching is meant to give life; it can kill. The preacher holds the keys; he can lock as well as unlock. Preaching is God’s great institution for planting spiritual life and bringing it to maturity. Done rightly, its benefits are beyond counting; done wrongly, nothing can be worse than the damage it does. It is easy to destroy the flock if the shepherd is careless or the pasture is ruined; easy to capture the fortress if the watchmen are asleep or the food and water are poisoned. Preaching carries such gracious privileges, is exposed to such great evils and involves so many serious responsibilities that it would be a mockery of the devil’s cunning, and a slander on his character and reputation, if he did not bring his most skillful influences to bear on corrupting the preacher and the preaching. In the face of all this, Paul’s exclaiming question, “Who is sufficient for these things?” is always in order.

Paul says: “Our sufficiency is of God, who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.” The true ministry is touched by God, enabled by God and made by God. The Spirit of God rests on the preacher in the power of His unction; the fruit of the Spirit is in his heart; the Spirit of God has brought both the man and the word to life. His preaching gives life — gives life as the spring gives life; gives life as the resurrection gives life; gives burning life as the summer gives burning life; gives fruitful life as the autumn gives fruitful life. The life-giving preacher is a man of God whose heart is always thirsting for God, whose soul is always following hard after God, whose eye is fixed on God alone, and in whom the flesh and the world have been crucified by the power of God’s Spirit. His ministry is like the generous flood of a life-giving river.

The preaching that kills is unspiritual preaching. Its ability does not come from God. Sources lower than God have given it its energy and its stimulus. The Spirit is not evident in the preacher or in his preaching. Preaching that kills may set many kinds of forces in motion and stir them up, but they are not spiritual forces. They may look like spiritual forces, but they are only the shadow, the counterfeit; they may seem to have life, but it is only the life of a magnet. The preaching that kills is the letter. It may be shapely and orderly, but it is still the letter — the dry, husky letter, the empty, bare shell. The letter may have the seed of life in it, but there is no breath of spring to call it out. These are winter seeds, as hard as the winter soil and as icy as the winter air; nothing thaws or sprouts from them. This letter-preaching has the truth. But even divine truth has no life-giving energy on its own; it must be energized by the Spirit, with all God’s forces behind it. Truth that the Spirit of God has not brought to life deadens as much as error does, or more. It may be truth without any mixture of error; but without the Spirit its shadow and touch are deadly, its truth becomes error and its light darkness. Letter-preaching has no unction; it is neither softened nor oiled by the Spirit. There may be tears, but tears cannot run God’s machinery; tears may be nothing more than a summer breeze blowing on a snow-covered iceberg — just slush on the surface. There may be feeling and earnestness, but it is the emotion of an actor and the earnestness of a lawyer. The preacher may be warmed by sparks he has lit himself, grow eloquent over his own interpretation of the text, and be earnest in delivering what his own brain has produced. The professor may take the apostle’s place and imitate his fire; brains and nerves may stand in for the work of God’s Spirit and pretend to do it. By these forces the letter may glow and sparkle like an illuminated manuscript, but the glow and sparkle will be as barren of life as a field sown with pearls. The death-dealing element lies behind the words, behind the sermon, behind the occasion, behind the manner, behind the delivery. The great hindrance is in the preacher himself. He does not have within himself the mighty forces that create life. There may be nothing lacking in his orthodoxy, honesty, purity or earnestness. Yet somehow the man — the inner man, in its secret places — has never broken down and surrendered to God, and his inner life is not a great highway for carrying God’s message and God’s power. Somehow self, and not God, rules in the holy of holies. Somewhere, without his knowing it at all, something that does not conduct the Spirit has touched his inner being, and the divine current has been stopped. His inner being has never felt how completely bankrupt it is spiritually, how utterly powerless; he has never learned to cry out with an inexpressible cry of self-despair and helplessness until God’s power and God’s fire come in and fill, purify and empower him. Self-esteem and self-reliance, in some destructive form, have defiled and violated the temple that ought to be kept sacred for God. Life-giving preaching costs the preacher a great deal — death to self, crucifixion to the world, the labor pains of his own soul. Only crucified preaching can give life. And crucified preaching can come only from a crucified man.

fields.title: The Letter Killeth
fields.body_html:
During this illness I was led to examine my life in the light of eternity more closely than I had done while I was enjoying good health. As I examined how I had carried out my duties toward my fellow creatures as a man, a Christian minister and an officer of the Church, my own conscience approved me; but when it came to my Redeemer and Saviour, the result was different. My return of gratitude and loving obedience bears no proportion to what I owe Him for redeeming, preserving and supporting me through all the ups and downs of life from infancy to old age. The coldness of my love toward Him who first loved me and has done so much for me overwhelmed and confused me. And to complete my unworthy character, I had not only failed to make use of the grace given me as fully as was my duty and privilege, but, for lack of using it, had — while abounding in perplexing cares and labors — fallen away from my first zeal and love. I was put to shame. I humbled myself, begged for mercy, and renewed my covenant to strive and to give myself without reserve to the Lord.—Bishop McKendree

The preaching that kills may be orthodox, and often is — dogmatically, unbreakably orthodox. We love orthodoxy. It is good. It is the best. It is the clean, clear-cut teaching of God’s Word, the trophies truth has won in its battle with error, the embankments faith has built against the devastating floods of misbelief and unbelief, whether honest or reckless. But orthodoxy that is as clear and hard as crystal, suspicious and combative, may be nothing more than the letter — well shaped, well named and well learned — the letter that kills. Nothing is as dead as a dead orthodoxy, too dead to speculate, too dead to think, to study or to pray.

The preaching that kills may have insight and a grasp of principles. It may be scholarly and critical in its taste. It may know every tiny detail of the derivation and grammar of the letter, be able to trim the letter into its perfect pattern, and shed light on it the way Plato and Cicero are illuminated. It may study it the way a lawyer studies his textbooks to prepare his brief or defend his case — and still be like a frost, a killing frost. Letter-preaching may be eloquent, polished with poetry and rhetoric, sprinkled with prayer, spiced with sensation and lit up by genius; and yet all of these may be only the massive or tasteful, expensive fittings and the rare and beautiful flowers that surround a corpse in its coffin. Or the preaching that kills may have no scholarship at all. It may show no freshness of thought or feeling, be dressed in tasteless generalities or empty particulars, with an uneven, sloppy style that has no flavour of either the prayer closet or the study, and is graced by neither thought, expression nor prayer. Under preaching like that, how wide and complete the desolation is! How deep the spiritual death!

This letter-preaching deals with the surface and shadow of things, and not with the things themselves. It does not get through to the inner part. It has no deep insight into the hidden life of God’s Word, and no strong grasp of it. It is true to the outside, but the outside is the husk, which must be broken open and gone through to reach the kernel. The letter may be dressed up to attract people and to be fashionable, but the attraction is not toward God, and the fashion is not for heaven. The failure lies in the preacher. God has not made him. He has never been in God’s hands like clay in the hands of the potter. He has been busy with the sermon — its thought and its finish, its appeal and its power to impress — but he has never sought, studied, sounded or experienced the deep things of God. fields.title: Tendencies to Be Avoided
fields.body_html:
Let us often look at Brainerd in the woods of America, pouring out his very soul before God for the perishing heathen, without whose salvation nothing could make him happy. Prayer — secret, fervent, believing prayer — lies at the root of all personal godliness. A competent knowledge of the language of the place where a missionary lives, a gentle and winning temper, and a heart given up to God in private devotion — these, these are the attainments that, more than all knowledge or all other gifts, will fit us to become God’s instruments in the great work of human redemption.—Carey’s Brotherhood, Serampore

There are two extreme tendencies in the ministry. The first is to shut itself away from contact with the people. The monk and the hermit were examples of this; they shut themselves away from people in order to be more with God. They failed, of course. Our time with God is of use only as we spend its priceless benefits on others. Our age, whether among preachers or people, is not very intent on God. Our cravings do not run that way. We shut ourselves up in our studies and become students, bookworms, Bible worms, sermon-makers, known for our literature, our thought and our sermons; but the people and God — where are they? Out of heart, out of mind. Preachers who are great thinkers and great students must be the greatest of pray-ers, or else they will be the greatest of backsliders — heartless professionals, rationalists, less than the least of preachers in God’s estimation.

The other tendency is to make the ministry thoroughly popular. The preacher is no longer God’s man but a man of affairs, a man of the people. He does not pray, because his mission is to the people. If he can move the people, create interest — a sensation in favor of religion, an interest in Church work — he is satisfied. His personal relationship with God plays no part in his work. Prayer has little or no place in his plans. The disaster and ruin of a ministry like that cannot be calculated by earthly arithmetic. Whatever the preacher is in prayer to God, for himself and for his people, that is the measure of his power to do real good to people, of his true fruitfulness, and of his true faithfulness to God and to people, for time and for eternity.

It is impossible for the preacher to keep his spirit in harmony with the divine nature of his high calling without much prayer. It is a serious mistake to think that the preacher can keep himself in shape and fit for service simply by sticking to his duty and working faithfully at the tasks and routine of the ministry. Even sermon-making — constant and demanding as it is, whether as an art, a duty, a job or a pleasure — will absorb and harden the heart, and, if prayer is neglected, will draw it away from God. The scientist loses God in nature. The preacher may lose God in his sermon.

Prayer refreshes the preacher’s heart. It keeps it in tune with God and in sympathy with the people. It lifts his ministry out of the chilly air of a mere profession, makes routine fruitful, and moves every wheel with the ease and power of a divine unction.

Mr. Spurgeon says: “Of course the preacher is distinguished above all others as a man of prayer. He prays as an ordinary Christian, or else he would be a hypocrite. He prays more than ordinary Christians, or else he would be unfit for the office he has taken on. If you as ministers are not very prayerful, you are to be pitied. If you become slack in sacred devotion, not only will you need to be pitied, but your people too, and the day is coming when you will be ashamed and confounded. All our libraries and studies are mere emptiness compared with our prayer closets. Our seasons of fasting and prayer at the Tabernacle have been high days indeed; never has heaven’s gate stood wider open; never have our hearts been nearer the central Glory.”

The praying that makes a prayerful ministry is not a little praying added in, the way we add flavouring to give something a pleasant taste. The praying must be in the body itself; it must form the blood and bones. Prayer is no petty duty pushed into a corner. It is not a piecemeal performance made up of scraps of time snatched from business and the other engagements of life. It means that the best of our time, the heart of our time and strength, must be given to it. It does not mean the prayer closet absorbed into the study or swallowed up in the busy duties of the ministry. It means the closet first and the study and activities second — with both the study and the activities refreshed and made effective by the closet. Prayer that affects a person’s ministry must set the tone of their life. The praying that gives color and direction to character is no pleasant, hurried pastime. It must enter as deeply into the heart and life as Christ’s “strong crying and tears” did. It must draw out the soul into an agony of desire, as Paul’s did. It must be a fire and a force worked deep within, like the “effectual, fervent prayer” of James. It must be of the kind that, when it is put into the golden censer and offered as incense before God, brings about mighty spiritual upheavals and revolutions.

Prayer is not a little habit pinned on us while we were tied to our mother’s apron strings. Nor is it a decent little quarter-minute grace said over an hour-long dinner. It is the most serious work of our most serious years. It takes up more of our time and appetite than our longest dinners or richest feasts. The prayer that makes much of our preaching must itself be made much of. The character of our praying will determine the character of our preaching. Light praying will make light preaching. Prayer makes preaching strong, gives it unction and makes it stick. In every ministry that has carried real weight for good, prayer has always been serious business.

The preacher must be, above everything, a man of prayer. His heart must graduate in the school of prayer. Only in the school of prayer can the heart learn to preach. No learning can make up for failing to pray. No earnestness, no diligence, no study, no gifts will make up for its absence.

Talking to people for God is a great thing, but talking to God for people is greater still. No one will ever talk well, and with real success, to people for God who has not learned well how to talk to God for people. More than this, prayerless words, in the pulpit and out of it, are deadening words.

fields.title: Prayer, the Great Essential
fields.body_html:
You know the value of prayer: it is precious beyond all price. Never, never neglect it.—Sir Thomas Buxton

Prayer is the first thing, the second thing and the third thing a minister needs. So pray, my dear brother: pray, pray, pray.—Edward Payson

Prayer, in the preacher’s life, in the preacher’s study and in the preacher’s pulpit, must be a prominent force that soaks into everything and an ingredient that colors everything. It must play no secondary part and be no mere outer coating. It is given to him to be with his Lord “all night in prayer.” To train himself in self-denying prayer, the preacher is told to look to his Master, who, “rising up a great while before day, went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.” The preacher’s study ought to be a prayer closet, a Bethel, an altar, a vision and a ladder, so that every thought might rise toward heaven before it went out toward people, and every part of the sermon might carry the scent of heaven’s air and be made serious, because God was in the study.

Just as an engine never moves until the fire is lit, so preaching — with all its machinery, perfection and polish — stands completely still, as far as spiritual results are concerned, until prayer has lit the fire and raised the steam. The texture, refinement and strength of the sermon are so much rubbish unless the mighty drive of prayer is in it, through it and behind it. By prayer the preacher must put God into the sermon. By prayer the preacher must move God toward the people before he can move the people toward God by his words. The preacher must have had an audience with God and ready access to Him before he can have access to the people. An open way to God for the preacher is the surest guarantee of an open way to the people.

It needs to be said again and again that prayer as a mere habit, as a performance gone through by routine or in a professional way, is a dead and rotten thing. Praying like that has nothing to do with the praying we are pleading for. We are stressing true praying — praying that engages every high part of the preacher’s being and sets it on fire. It is prayer born of a living oneness with Christ and of the fullness of the Holy Ghost. It springs from the deep, overflowing fountains of tender compassion and of an undying concern for people’s eternal good; from a consuming zeal for the glory of God; and from a thorough conviction of how difficult and delicate the preacher’s work is and how urgently he needs God’s mightiest help. Praying grounded on these solemn and deep convictions is the only true praying. Preaching backed by praying like this is the only preaching that sows the seeds of eternal life in human hearts and builds people up for heaven.

It is true that there can be popular preaching, pleasant preaching, attractive preaching, preaching with great intellectual, literary and mental force — with its own measure and kind of good — and with little or no praying behind it. But the preaching that achieves God’s purpose in preaching must be born of prayer, from the text to the introduction. It must be delivered with the energy and spirit of prayer. And it must be followed up by the preacher’s prayers, which make it sprout and keep it a living force in the hearts of the hearers long after the occasion has passed.

We may explain away the spiritual poverty of our preaching in many ways, but the real secret will be found in our lack of urgent prayer for God’s presence in the power of the Holy Spirit. There are countless preachers who can deliver masterly sermons of their kind; but the effects are short-lived. They do not enter as a factor at all into the realm of the spirit, where the fearful war between God and Satan, heaven and hell, is being fought, because prayer has not made them powerfully militant and spiritually victorious.

The preachers who win mighty results for God are the men who have prevailed in pleading with God before they venture to plead with people. The preachers who are mightiest with God in their prayer closets are mightiest with people in their pulpits.

Preachers are human beings, and they are exposed to the strong drift of human currents and are often caught by it. Praying is spiritual work, and human nature does not like demanding spiritual work. Human nature wants to sail to heaven with a favorable breeze on a full, smooth sea. Prayer is humbling work. It brings down intellect and pride, crucifies vanity and signs the declaration of our spiritual bankruptcy — and all of these are hard for flesh and blood to bear. It is easier not to pray than to bear them. So we come to one of the crying evils of our times, maybe of all times: little or no praying. Of these two evils, perhaps little praying is worse than no praying. Little praying is a kind of make-believe, a soothing ointment for the conscience, a farce and a delusion.

How little we value prayer is plain from how little time we give it. The time the average preacher gives to prayer hardly counts in the total of his day. Quite often the preacher’s only praying is done by his bedside in his nightclothes, ready for bed and soon in it — with, perhaps, a few hasty snatches of prayer added before he is dressed in the morning. How feeble, empty and small such praying is compared with the time and energy holy men, in the Bible and outside it, have given to prayer! How poor and mean our petty, childish praying looks beside the habits of the true men of God in every age! It is to men who regard praying as their main business, and who give time to it in keeping with this high view of its importance, that God entrusts the keys of His kingdom, and it is through them that He works His spiritual wonders in this world. Great praying is the sign and seal of God’s great leaders, and the pledge of the conquering forces with which God will crown their labors.

The preacher is commissioned to pray as well as to preach. His mission is incomplete if he does not do both well. The preacher may speak with all the eloquence of men and of angels; but unless he can pray with a faith that draws all heaven to his help, his preaching will be “as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal” as far as any lasting, God-honoring, soul-saving use is concerned.

fields.title: A Praying Ministry Successful
fields.body_html:
The main cause of my leanness and unfruitfulness is an unaccountable reluctance to pray. I can write or read or talk or listen with a ready heart; but prayer is more spiritual and inward than any of these, and the more spiritual a duty is, the more my carnal heart tends to shy away from it. Prayer and patience and faith are never disappointed. I learned long ago that if I was ever to be a minister, faith and prayer must make me one. When I can find my heart in the right frame and free for prayer, everything else is comparatively easy.—Richard Newton

It can be laid down as a spiritual axiom that in every truly successful ministry prayer is an evident and controlling force — evident and controlling in the life of the preacher, and evident and controlling in the deep spirituality of his work. A ministry may be a very thoughtful ministry without prayer. The preacher may win fame and popularity without prayer. The whole machinery of the preacher’s life and work may run without the oil of prayer, or with barely enough to grease one cog. But no ministry can be a spiritual one, producing holiness in the preacher and in his people, unless prayer is made an evident and controlling force.

The preacher who truly prays puts God into the work. God does not come into the preacher’s work automatically or on general principles; He comes through prayer and special urgency. It is as true of the preacher as of the penitent sinner that God will be found by us on the day we seek Him with our whole heart. A prayerful ministry is the only ministry that brings the preacher into sympathy with the people. Prayer unites us to the human just as truly as it unites us to the divine. A prayerful ministry is the only ministry fit for the high offices and responsibilities of the preacher. Colleges, learning, books, theology and preaching cannot make a preacher, but praying does. The apostles’ commission to preach was a blank until it was filled in by the Pentecost that praying brought. A prayerful minister has gone beyond the realm of the popular, beyond the man of mere affairs and worldly business and pulpit attractiveness, beyond the church organizer or administrator, into a more sublime and mightier realm — the realm of the spiritual. Holiness is the product of his work; transformed hearts and lives display the reality of his work, its genuineness and its substance. God is with him. His ministry is not driven by worldly or superficial principles. He is richly stocked with the things of God and deeply schooled in them. His long, deep communion with God about his people, and the agony of his wrestling spirit, have crowned him a prince in the things of God. The iciness of the mere professional melted long ago under the intensity of his praying.

The shallow results of many ministries, and the deadness of others, are explained by a lack of praying. No ministry can succeed without much praying, and this praying must be fundamental, constant and always increasing. The text and the sermon should be the result of prayer. The study should be bathed in prayer, all its duties soaked through with prayer, and its whole spirit the spirit of prayer. “I am sorry that I have prayed so little,” was the deathbed regret of one of God’s chosen servants — a sad and remorseful regret for a preacher. “I want a life of greater, deeper, truer prayer,” said the late Archbishop Tait. We may all say the same, and we may all obtain it.

God’s true preachers have been marked by one great feature: they were men of prayer. Though they often differed in many things, they have always had a common center. They may have started from different points and traveled by different roads, but they all came together at one point: they were one in prayer. To them God was the center of attraction, and prayer was the path that led to God. These men did not pray now and then, or a little at regular times or odd moments. They prayed in such a way that their prayers entered into their characters and shaped them. They prayed in such a way as to affect their own lives and the lives of others. They prayed in such a way as to make the history of the Church and influence the current of their times. They spent much time in prayer, not because they were watching the shadow on the sundial or the hands on the clock, but because prayer was such a momentous and absorbing business to them that they could hardly bring themselves to stop.

To them prayer was what it was to Paul — a striving with earnest effort of soul; what it was to Jacob — a wrestling and prevailing; what it was to Christ — “strong crying and tears.” They “prayed always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance.” “The effectual, fervent prayer” has been the mightiest weapon of God’s mightiest soldiers. What is said of Elijah — that he “was a man subject to like passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain: and it rained not on the earth by the space of three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth brought forth her fruit” — sums up all the prophets and preachers who have moved their generation for God, and shows the instrument by which they worked their wonders.

fields.title: Much Time Should Be Given to Prayer
fields.body_html:
The great masters and teachers of Christian doctrine have always found in prayer their highest source of illumination. Without going beyond the bounds of the English Church, it is recorded of Bishop Andrewes that he spent five hours a day on his knees. The greatest practical resolutions that have enriched and beautified human life in Christian times have been reached in prayer.—Canon Liddon

Many private prayers must, by their very nature, be short. Public prayers, as a rule, ought to be short and concise. There is plenty of room for brief, spontaneous prayers, and they are rightly valued. Yet in our private communion with God, time is essential to its value. Much time spent with God is the secret of all successful praying. Prayer that is felt as a mighty force is the product, directly or indirectly, of much time spent with God. Our short prayers owe their point and effectiveness to the long ones that came before them. No one can pray the short, prevailing prayer who has not prevailed with God in a mightier and longer struggle. Jacob’s victory of faith could not have been won without that all-night wrestling. We do not get to know God by dropping in on Him. God does not give His gifts to casual or hurried visitors who come and go. Being much alone with God is the secret of knowing Him and of having influence with Him. He yields to the persistence of a faith that knows Him. He gives His richest gifts to those who show how much they desire and value those gifts by the constancy as well as the earnestness of their persistent asking. Christ, who is our Example in this as in other things, spent many whole nights in prayer. It was His habit to pray much. He had His usual place to pray. Many long seasons of prayer make up His history and character. Paul prayed night and day. Daniel had to take time from very important affairs to pray three times a day. David’s praying, morning, noon and night, was no doubt often very long. We have no exact record of the time these Bible saints spent in prayer, but the signs are that they spent a great deal of time in it, and that on some occasions long seasons of prayer were their custom.

We would not want anyone to think that the value of their prayers is to be measured by the clock. Our purpose is to impress on our minds how necessary it is to be much alone with God — and that if our faith has not produced this feature in us, then our faith is of a feeble and superficial kind.

The men who have most fully shown Christ in their character, and who have most powerfully influenced the world for Him, have been men who spent so much time with God that it became a notable feature of their lives. Charles Simeon gave the hours from four to eight in the morning to God. Mr. Wesley spent two hours a day in prayer. He began at four in the morning. Someone who knew him well wrote of him: “He thought prayer to be more his business than anything else, and I have seen him come out of his prayer closet with a serenity of face next to shining.” John Fletcher stained the walls of his room with the breath of his prayers. Sometimes he would pray all night; he prayed always, frequently, and with great earnestness. His whole life was a life of prayer. “I would not rise from my seat,” he said, “without lifting my heart to God.” His greeting to a friend was always: “Do I meet you praying?” Luther said: “If I fail to spend two hours in prayer each morning, the devil gets the victory through the day. I have so much business that I cannot get on without spending three hours a day in prayer.” He had a motto: “He who has prayed well has studied well.”

Archbishop Leighton was alone with God so much that he seemed to be in constant meditation. “Prayer and praise were his business and his pleasure,” says his biographer. Bishop Ken was with God so much that his soul was said to be in love with God. He was with God every morning before the clock struck three. Bishop Asbury said: “I intend to rise at four o’clock as often as I can and spend two hours in prayer and meditation.” Samuel Rutherford, the fragrance of whose godliness is still rich, rose at three in the morning to meet God in prayer. Joseph Alleine got up at four o’clock for his business of praying, which went on until eight. If he heard other tradesmen at work at their business before he was up, he would exclaim: “Oh, how this shames me! Does not my Master deserve more than theirs?” Whoever has learned this trade well can draw on heaven’s unfailing bank at will, on sight, and be honored there.

One of the holiest and most gifted of Scottish preachers says: “I ought to spend the best hours in communion with God. It is my noblest and most fruitful work, and it is not to be pushed into a corner. The morning hours, from six to eight, are the most free from interruption and should be used this way. After tea is my best hour, and that should be solemnly dedicated to God. I ought not to give up the good old habit of prayer before going to bed; but I must guard against sleep. When I wake in the night, I ought to get up and pray. A little time after breakfast might be given to intercession.” This was Robert McCheyne’s plan for prayer. The memorable Methodist band puts us to shame by their praying: “From four to five in the morning, private prayer; from five to six in the evening, private prayer.”

John Welch, the holy and wonderful Scottish preacher, thought a day badly spent if he did not spend eight or ten hours of it in prayer. He kept a plaid blanket so that he could wrap himself in it when he got up to pray at night. His wife would complain when she found him lying on the ground weeping. He would reply: “O woman, I have the souls of three thousand to answer for, and I do not know how it is with many of them!”

fields.title: Examples of Praying Men
fields.body_html:
The act of praying is the very highest energy the human mind is capable of — praying, that is, with all the faculties totally concentrated. The great mass of worldly people and of learned people are absolutely incapable of prayer.—Samuel Taylor Coleridge

Bishop Wilson says: “In H. Martyn’s journal, the spirit of prayer, the time he gave to the duty and his fervor in it are the first things that strike me.”

Payson wore grooves into the hardwood floorboards where his knees pressed so often and for so long. His biographer says: “His continuing constant in prayer, whatever his circumstances, is the most noticeable fact in his history, and it points out the duty of all who would equal his eminence. His outstanding and almost uninterrupted success must no doubt be credited in large measure to his ardent and persevering prayers.”

The Marquis de Renty, to whom Christ was most precious, told his servant to call him from his devotions at the end of half an hour. When the time came, the servant saw his face through an opening. It was marked with such holiness that he hated to disturb him. His lips were moving, but he made no sound at all. The servant waited until three half-hours had passed. Then he called him, and the Marquis rose from his knees, saying that the half-hour was so short when he was communing with Christ.

Brainerd said: “I love to be alone in my cottage, where I can spend much time in prayer.”

William Bramwell is famous in Methodist history for his personal holiness, for his wonderful success in preaching and for the marvelous answers to his prayers. He would pray for hours at a time. He almost lived on his knees. He went around his circuits like a flame of fire. The fire was lit by the time he spent in prayer. He often spent as much as four hours in a single season of prayer alone.

Bishop Andrewes spent the greater part of five hours every day in prayer and devotion.

Sir Henry Havelock always spent the first two hours of each day alone with God. If the camp was to be broken at 6 a.m., he would get up at four.

Earl Cairns got up every day at six o’clock so that he could have an hour and a half for studying the Bible and for prayer before leading family worship at a quarter to eight.

Dr. Judson’s success in prayer can be traced to the fact that he gave much time to prayer. He says on this point: “Arrange your affairs, if possible, so that you can devote two or three hours every day, without hurrying, not merely to devotional exercises but to the very act of secret prayer and communion with God. Try seven times a day to withdraw from business and company and lift up your soul to God in private. Begin the day by rising after midnight and devoting some time, in the silence and darkness of the night, to this sacred work. Let the hour of dawn find you at the same work. Let the hours of nine, twelve, three, six, and nine at night see the same. Be resolute in His cause. Make every sacrifice you practically can to keep it up. Remember that your time is short, and that business and company must not be allowed to rob you of your God.” Impossible, we say — fanatical instructions! Yet Dr. Judson stamped an empire for Christ and laid the foundations of God’s kingdom in imperishable granite in the heart of Burma. He was successful — one of the few men who have powerfully impressed the world for Christ. Many men of greater gifts, genius and learning than he have made no such impression; their religious work is like footprints in the sand, but he engraved his work on diamond-hard rock. The secret of its depth and endurance is found in the fact that he gave time to prayer. He kept the iron red-hot with prayer, and God’s skill shaped it with lasting power. No one can do a great and lasting work for God who is not a man of prayer, and no one can be a man of prayer who does not give much time to praying.

Is it true that prayer is simply going along with a habit, dull and mechanical? A petty performance we are trained into until tameness, brevity and superficiality are its main ingredients? “Is it true that prayer is, as is assumed, little more than the half-passive play of sentiment that drifts lazily on through the minutes or hours of easy daydreaming?” Canon Liddon continues: “Let those who have really prayed give the answer. Sometimes, like the patriarch Jacob, they describe prayer as a wrestling with an Unseen Power that may last, not rarely in an earnest life, late into the night or even until daybreak. Sometimes, like St. Paul, they speak of united intercession as a joint struggle. When they pray, their eyes are fixed on the Great Intercessor in Gethsemane, on the drops of blood that fall to the ground in that agony of resignation and sacrifice. Persistence is of the essence of successful prayer. Persistence means not dreaminess but sustained work. It is especially through prayer that the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence and the violent take it by force.” It was a saying of the late Bishop Hamilton that “No one is likely to do much good in prayer who does not begin by looking on it as a work to be prepared for and persevered in with all the earnestness we bring to the subjects we consider at once most interesting and most necessary.”

fields.title: Begin the Day with Prayer
fields.body_html:
I ought to pray before seeing anyone. Often, when I sleep long or meet with others early, it is eleven or twelve o’clock before I begin secret prayer. This is a wretched system. It is unscriptural. Christ rose before daylight and went to a solitary place. David says: “Early will I seek thee”; “Thou shalt early hear my voice.” Family prayer loses much of its power and sweetness, and I can do no good to those who come seeking help from me. My conscience feels guilty, my soul unfed, my lamp untrimmed. Then, when I do come to secret prayer, my soul is often out of tune. I feel it is far better to begin with God — to see His face first, to get my soul near Him before it is near anyone else.—Robert Murray McCheyne

The men who have done the most for God in this world have been on their knees early. Whoever fritters away the early morning — its opportunity and its freshness — on pursuits other than seeking God will make poor progress seeking Him for the rest of the day. If God is not first in our thoughts and efforts in the morning, He will be in last place for the remainder of the day.

Behind this early rising and early praying is the ardent desire that drives us on in this pursuit of God. Listlessness in the morning is the sign of a listless heart. The heart that is slow to seek God in the morning has lost its taste for God. David’s heart burned for God. He hungered and thirsted for God, and so he sought God early, before daylight. fields.title: Prayer and Devotion United
fields.body_html:
There is an obvious lack of spiritual influence on the ministry of our day. I feel it in my own case and I see it in others. I am afraid there is too much of a low, managing, scheming, maneuvering frame of mind among us. We are going out of our way more than is wise to suit one person’s taste and another person’s prejudices. The ministry is a grand and holy affair, and it should find in us a simple habit of spirit and a holy but humble indifference to all consequences. The chief defect in Christian ministers is the lack of a devotional habit.—Richard Cecil

There has never been a greater need for saintly men and women, and the call for saintly, God-devoted preachers is more urgent still. The world is moving with giant strides. Satan has his grip and his rule on the world, and he works to make all its movements serve his ends. Religion must do its best work and present its most attractive and perfect models. By every means, modern sainthood must be inspired by the loftiest ideals and by the greatest possibilities that come through the Spirit. Paul lived on his knees so that the Ephesian Church might measure the heights, breadths and depths of a saintliness beyond measure, and “be filled with all the fullness of God.” Epaphras gave himself to the exhausting toil and strenuous conflict of fervent prayer, so that the Colossian Church might “stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.” Everywhere in apostolic times, everything was strained to the utmost so that the people of God might each and “all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” No prize was given to dwarfs; no encouragement to an old age that was still infancy. The babies were to grow; and the old, instead of feebleness and infirmities, were to bear fruit in old age and be fat and flourishing. The most divine thing in religion is holy men and holy women.

No amount of money, genius or culture can move things for God. Holiness energizing the soul, the whole person ablaze with love, with desire for more faith, more prayer, more zeal, more consecration — this is the secret of power. These we need and must have, and men must be the living embodiment of this God-kindled devotion. For lack of them, God’s advance has been halted, His cause crippled and His name dishonored. Genius, however lofty and gifted; education, however learned and refined; position, dignity, rank, honored names, high church officials — none of these can move this chariot of our God. It is a fiery chariot, and only fiery forces can move it. The genius of a Milton fails. The imperial strength of a Leo fails. Brainerd’s spirit can move it. Brainerd’s spirit was on fire for God, on fire for souls. Nothing earthly, worldly or selfish came in to lessen in the least the intensity of this all-driving and all-consuming force and flame.

Prayer is the creator as well as the channel of devotion. The spirit of devotion is the spirit of prayer. Prayer and devotion are united as soul and body are united, as life and the heart are united. There is no real prayer without devotion, and no devotion without prayer. The preacher must be surrendered to God in the holiest devotion. He is not a professional man; his ministry is not a profession. It is a divine institution, a divine devotion. He is devoted to God. His aims, aspirations and ambition are for God and toward God, and to such a man prayer is as essential as food is to life.

The preacher, above everything else, must be devoted to God. The preacher’s relationship with God is the badge and the credentials of his ministry. These must be clear, conclusive and unmistakable. No ordinary, superficial kind of godliness will do for him. If he does not excel in grace, he does not excel at all. If he does not preach by his life, character and conduct, he does not preach at all. If his godliness is light, his preaching may be as soft and sweet as music and as gifted as Apollo, yet its weight will be a feather’s weight — dreamy, passing away like the morning cloud or the early dew. Devotion to God — there is no substitute for this in the preacher’s character and conduct. Devotion to a Church, to opinions, to an organization, to orthodoxy — these are paltry, misleading and empty when they become the source of inspiration and the driving motive of a call. God must be the mainspring of the preacher’s effort, the fountain and crown of all his toil. The name and honor of Jesus Christ and the advance of His cause must be all in all. The preacher must have no inspiration but the name of Jesus Christ, no ambition but to have Him glorified, no toil but for Him. Then prayer will be a source of his insight, the means of constant progress and the measure of his success. The constant aim — the only ambition — the preacher can cherish is to have God with him.

Never has the cause of God needed perfect demonstrations of the possibilities of prayer more than in this age. No age and no person will be examples of the gospel’s power except the ages or people of deep and earnest prayer. A prayerless age will have only scant models of divine power. Prayerless hearts will never climb to these Alpine heights. Our age may be better than past ages, but there is an infinite distance between an age made better by the force of advancing civilization and an age made better by an increase of holiness and Christlikeness through the energy of prayer. The Jews were much better off when Christ came than in the ages before. It was the golden age of their Pharisaic religion. Their golden religious age crucified Christ. Never more praying, never less praying; never more sacrifices, never less sacrifice; never less idolatry, never more idolatry; never more temple worship, never less worship of God; never more lip service, never less heart service (God worshiped by lips whose hearts and hands crucified God’s Son!); never more churchgoers, never fewer saints.

It is the force of prayer that makes saints. Holy characters are formed by the power of real praying. The more true saints, the more praying; the more praying, the more true saints.

fields.title: An Example of Devotion
fields.body_html:
I urge on you communion with Christ — a growing communion. There are curtains in Christ still to be drawn aside that we have never seen behind, and new folds of love in Him. I despair of ever reaching the far end of that love, there are so many layers in it. So dig deep, and sweat and labor and take pains for Him, and set aside as much time in the day for Him as you can. We will be won over in the labor.—Samuel Rutherford

God has now, and has always had, many of these devoted, prayerful preachers — men in whose lives prayer has been a mighty, controlling, conspicuous force. The world has felt their power; God has felt and honored their power; God’s cause has moved mightily and swiftly through their prayers; and holiness has shone out in their characters with a divine radiance.

God found one of the men He was looking for in David Brainerd, whose work and name have passed into history. He was no ordinary man. He was capable of shining in any company, the equal of the wise and gifted, and eminently suited to fill the most attractive pulpits and to labor among the refined and cultured, who were so eager to have him as their pastor. President Edwards testifies that he was “a young man of distinguished talents, had extraordinary knowledge of men and things, had rare conversational powers, excelled in his knowledge of theology, and was truly, for one so young, an extraordinary divine, especially in all matters relating to experiential religion. I never knew his equal, for his age and standing, in clear and accurate ideas of the nature and essence of true religion. His manner in prayer was almost impossible to imitate, such as I have very rarely known equaled. His learning was very considerable, and he had extraordinary gifts for the pulpit.”

No more sublime story has been recorded in earthly history than that of David Brainerd; no miracle testifies with more divine force to the truth of Christianity than the life and work of such a man. He was alone in the savage wilderness of America, struggling day and night with a fatal disease, untrained in the care of souls, and for much of the time able to reach the Indians only through the clumsy medium of a pagan interpreter. Yet with the Word of God in his heart and in his hand, his soul fired with the divine flame, and a place and time to pour out his soul to God in prayer, he fully established the worship of God and secured all its gracious results. The Indians were changed with a great change — from the lowest degradation of an ignorant and debased heathenism to pure, devout, intelligent Christians. Every vice was reformed; the outward duties of Christianity were at once embraced and practiced; family prayer was set up; the Sabbath was established and religiously kept; and the inward graces of religion were displayed with growing sweetness and strength. The explanation of these results is found in David Brainerd himself — not in circumstances or chance, but in the man Brainerd. He was God’s man, for God first and last and all the time. God could flow through him unhindered. The almighty power of grace was neither stopped nor narrowed by the condition of his heart. The whole channel had been widened and cleaned out for God’s fullest and most powerful passage, so that God, with all His mighty forces, could come down on that hopeless, savage wilderness and transform it into His blooming and fruitful garden. For nothing is too hard for God to do if He can get the right kind of man to do it with.

Brainerd lived a life of holiness and prayer. His diary is full — monotonously full — of the record of his seasons of fasting, meditation and withdrawal. The time he spent in private prayer amounted to many hours a day. “When I return home,” he said, “and give myself to meditation, prayer and fasting, my soul longs for mortification, self-denial, humility and separation from all things of the world.” “I have nothing to do with earth,” he said, “except to labor in it honestly for God. I do not desire to live one minute for anything the earth can offer.” This is the high order on which he prayed: “Feeling something of the sweetness of communion with God and the constraining force of His love, and how wonderfully it captivates the soul and makes all the desires and affections center on God, I set apart this day for secret fasting and prayer, to ask God to direct and bless me with regard to the great work I have in view of preaching the gospel, and that the Lord would return to me and show me the light of His face. I had little life and power in the morning. Near the middle of the afternoon God enabled me to wrestle ardently in intercession for my absent friends; but just at nightfall the Lord visited me marvelously in prayer. I think my soul was never in such agony before. I felt no restraint, for the treasures of divine grace were opened to me. I wrestled for absent friends, for the gathering in of souls, for multitudes of poor souls, and for many people in many distant places whom I took to be children of God. I was in such agony, from when the sun was half an hour high until nearly dark, that I was wet with sweat all over; and yet it seemed to me that I had done nothing. Oh, my dear Saviour sweated blood for poor souls! I longed for more compassion toward them. I still felt in a sweet frame of mind, under a sense of divine love and grace, and went to bed in that frame, with my heart set on God.” It was prayer that gave his life and ministry their marvelous power.

The men of mighty prayer are men of spiritual might. Prayers never die. Brainerd’s whole life was a life of prayer. He prayed by day and by night. He prayed before preaching and after preaching. Riding through the endless solitude of the forests, he prayed. On his bed of straw, he prayed. Withdrawing into the dense and lonely forests, he prayed. Hour by hour, day after day, early in the morning and late at night, he was praying and fasting, pouring out his soul, interceding and communing with God. He was with God mightily in prayer, and God was mightily with him. And by it he, being dead, yet speaketh and worketh, and he will speak and work until the end comes; and among the glorious ones of that glorious day he will be with the first.

Jonathan Edwards says of him: “His life shows the right way to success in the work of the ministry. He sought it as a soldier seeks victory in a siege or a battle, or as a man running a race for a great prize. Moved by love for Christ and for souls, how did he labor? Always fervently. Not only in word and doctrine, in public and in private, but in prayers by day and night, wrestling with God in secret and travailing in birth with unutterable groans and agonies, until Christ was formed in the hearts of the people to whom he was sent. Like a true son of Jacob, he persevered in wrestling through all the darkness of the night, until the breaking of the day!”

fields.title: Heart Preparation Necessary
fields.body_html:
For nothing reaches the heart except what comes from the heart, and nothing pierces the conscience except what comes from a living conscience.—William Penn

This morning I was more taken up with preparing my head than my heart. This has often been my mistake, and I have always felt the harm of it, especially in prayer. Correct it, then, O Lord! Enlarge my heart and I shall preach.—Robert Murray McCheyne

A sermon that has more head than heart poured into it will not be carried home with effect to the hearers.—Richard Cecil

Prayer, with its many and many-sided forces, helps the mouth to speak the truth in its fullness and freedom. The preacher is to be prayed for; the preacher is made by prayer. The preacher’s mouth is to be prayed for; his mouth is to be opened and filled by prayer. A holy mouth is made by praying, by much praying; a bold mouth is made by praying, by much praying. The Church and the world, God and heaven, owe much to Paul’s mouth; and Paul’s mouth owed its power to prayer.

How many-sided, how limitless, how valuable and how helpful prayer is to the preacher — in so many ways, at so many points, in every way! One great value is that it helps his heart.

Praying makes the preacher a heart preacher. Prayer puts the preacher’s heart into the preacher’s sermon; prayer puts the preacher’s sermon into the preacher’s heart.

The heart makes the preacher. Men with great hearts are great preachers. Men with bad hearts may do some good, but it is rare. The hired hand and the stranger may help the sheep at some points, but it is the good shepherd, with the good shepherd’s heart, who will bless the sheep and fill the shepherd’s place in full measure.

We have emphasized sermon preparation until we have lost sight of the important thing that needs preparing — the heart. A prepared heart is much better than a prepared sermon. A prepared heart will make a prepared sermon.

Volumes have been written setting out the mechanics and style of sermon-making, until we have become possessed by the idea that this scaffolding is the building. The young preacher has been taught to spend all his strength on the form, style and beauty of his sermon as a mechanical and intellectual product. fields.title: Grace from the Heart Rather than the Head
fields.body_html:
Do not strive to be a fine preacher. Jerichos are blown down with rams’ horns. Look simply to Jesus for food to preach; and what is needed will be given, and what is given will be blessed, whether it is a grain of barley or a wheat loaf, a crust or a crumb. Your mouth will be a flowing stream or a sealed fountain, depending on the state of your heart. Avoid all controversy in preaching, talking or writing; preach nothing down but the devil, and nothing up but Jesus Christ.—Berridge

The heart is the Saviour of the world. Heads do not save. Genius, brains, brilliance, strength and natural gifts do not save. The gospel flows through hearts. All the mightiest forces are heart forces. All the sweetest and loveliest graces are heart graces. Great hearts make great characters; great hearts make divine characters. God is love. There is nothing greater than love, nothing greater than God. Hearts make heaven; heaven is love. There is nothing higher and nothing sweeter than heaven. It is the heart and not the head that makes God’s great preachers. The heart counts for much in every way in religion. The heart must speak from the pulpit. The heart must listen in the pew. In fact, we serve God with our hearts. Homage from the head is not accepted currency in heaven.

We believe that one of the serious and most widespread errors of the modern pulpit is putting more thought than prayer, and more head than heart, into its sermons. Big hearts make big preachers; good hearts make good preachers. A theological school to enlarge and cultivate the heart is the golden need of the gospel. The pastor binds his people to himself and rules them by his heart. They may admire his gifts, they may be proud of his ability, they may be moved for the moment by his sermons; but the stronghold of his power is his heart. His scepter is love. The throne of his power is his heart.

The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep. Heads never make martyrs. It is the heart that surrenders life to love and faithfulness. It takes great courage to be a faithful pastor, but only the heart can supply that courage. Gifts and genius may be brave, but it is the gifts and genius of the heart, not of the head.

It is easier to fill the head than to prepare the heart. It is easier to make a brain sermon than a heart sermon. It was the heart that drew the Son of God from heaven. It is the heart that will draw people to heaven. What the world needs is men of heart — to sympathize with its woe, to kiss away its sorrows, to show compassion on its misery and to ease its pain. Christ was above all the man of sorrows, because He was above all the man of heart.

“Give me thy heart,” is God’s demand of people. “Give me thy heart!” is what people demand of one another.

A professional ministry is a heartless ministry. When salary plays a large part in the ministry, the heart plays a small part. We may make preaching our business and not put our hearts into the business. Whoever puts self at the front of his preaching puts heart at the back. Whoever does not sow with his heart in his study will never reap a harvest for God. The prayer closet is the heart’s study. We will learn more there about how to preach and what to preach than we can learn in our libraries. “Jesus wept” is the shortest and the biggest verse in the Bible. It is he who goes forth weeping (not preaching great sermons), bearing precious seed, who shall come again rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

Praying gives good sense, brings wisdom, and broadens and strengthens the mind. The prayer closet is a perfect teacher and schoolhouse for the preacher. Thought is not only brightened and clarified in prayer; thought is born in prayer. We can learn more in an hour of prayer — when it is real prayer — than in many hours in the study. There are books in the prayer closet that can be found and read nowhere else. Revelations are given in the prayer closet that are given nowhere else.

fields.title: Unction a Necessity
fields.body_html:
One bright blessing that private prayer brings down on the ministry is an indescribable and inimitable something — an unction from the Holy One . . . . If the anointing we carry does not come from the Lord of hosts, we are deceivers, since only in prayer can we obtain it. Let us continue constant and fervent in supplication. Let your fleece lie on the threshing floor of supplication until it is wet with the dew of heaven.—Charles Haddon Spurgeon

Alexander Knox, a Christian philosopher of Wesley’s time — not a follower of Wesley, but a close personal friend, with much spiritual sympathy for the Wesleyan movement — writes: “It is strange and sad, but I truly believe it to be a fact that, except among the Methodists and Methodist-minded clergymen, there is not much interesting preaching in England. The clergy, all too generally, have completely lost the art. I believe there is, in the great laws of the moral world, a kind of secret understanding — like the affinities in chemistry — between religious truth rightly proclaimed and the deepest feelings of the human mind. Where the one is properly displayed, the other will respond. Did not our hearts burn within us? — but for this, devout feeling in the speaker is indispensable. Now, I am obliged to say from my own observation that this onction, as the French quite fittingly call it, is beyond all comparison more likely to be found in England in a Methodist meeting house than in a parish Church. This, and this alone, seems really to be what fills the Methodist houses and empties the Churches. I am, I truly think, no fanatic; I am a most sincere and warm-hearted churchman, a humble disciple of the school of Hale and Boyle, of Burnet and Leighton. Yet I must state that when I was in this country two years ago, I did not hear a single preacher who taught me as my own great masters did, except those who are considered Methodist-minded. And I now despair of getting an atom of heart instruction from any other quarter. The Methodist preachers (though I may not always approve of all their expressions) most certainly do spread this true religion and undefiled. I felt real pleasure last Sunday. I can testify that the preacher did indeed speak the words of truth and soberness. There was no eloquence — the honest man never dreamed of such a thing — but there was something far better: a heartfelt communication of living truth. I say living, because it was impossible not to feel that he lived on what he declared to others.”

This unction is the art of preaching. The preacher who never had this unction never had the art of preaching. The preacher who has lost this unction has lost the art of preaching. Whatever other arts he may have and keep — the art of sermon-making, the art of eloquence, the art of great, clear thinking, the art of pleasing an audience — he has lost the divine art of preaching. This unction makes God’s truth powerful and interesting. It draws and attracts, builds up, convicts and saves.

This unction brings God’s revealed truth to life, making it living and life-giving. Even God’s truth, spoken without this unction, is light, dead and deadening. It may be full of truth, weighty with thought, sparkling with rhetoric, sharpened by logic and powerful with earnestness; but without this divine unction it ends in death and not in life. Mr. Spurgeon says: “I wonder how long we might rack our brains before we could put into plain words what is meant by preaching with unction. Yet the one who preaches knows when it is present, and the one who listens soon detects when it is absent. Samaria in famine is a picture of a sermon without it. Jerusalem, with her feast of fat things full of marrow, may represent a sermon enriched by it. Everyone knows what the freshness of the morning is, when bright pearls of dew lie on every blade of grass; but who can describe it, much less produce it by himself? Such is the mystery of spiritual anointing. We know what it is, but we cannot tell others. It is as easy as it is foolish to counterfeit it. Unction is something you cannot manufacture, and its counterfeits are worse than worthless. Yet in itself it is priceless, and needed beyond measure if you want to build up believers and bring sinners to Christ.”
