fields.title: Unction, the Mark of True Gospel Preaching
fields.body_html:
Speak for eternity. Above all things, cultivate your own spirit. A word spoken by you when your conscience is clear and your heart is full of God’s Spirit is worth ten thousand words spoken in unbelief and sin. Remember that God, and not man, must have the glory. If the veil of the world’s machinery were lifted off, how much we would find is done in answer to the prayers of God’s children!—Robert Murray McCheyne

Unction is that indefinable, indescribable something that a renowned Scottish preacher of old described like this: “There is sometimes something in preaching that cannot be credited either to its matter or to its expression. No one can describe what it is or where it comes from, but with a sweet violence it pierces into the heart and the affections, and it comes directly from the Word. And if there is any way to obtain such a thing, it is through the heavenly disposition of the speaker.”

We call it unction. It is this unction that makes the word of God “quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” It is this unction that gives the preacher’s words such point, sharpness and power, and that creates such friction and stir in many a dead congregation. The same truths have been told strictly according to the letter, as smooth as human oil could make them — but with no signs of life, not a single pulse beat; everything as peaceful as the grave, and as dead. Then the same preacher receives a baptism of this unction. The divine breath is on him; the letter of the Word has been adorned and set on fire by this mysterious power; and the throbbings of life begin — life that receives, or life that resists. The unction pervades the conscience and convicts it, and it breaks the heart.

This divine unction is the feature that separates and distinguishes true gospel preaching from every other way of presenting the truth, and it creates a wide spiritual gulf between the preacher who has it and the one who does not. It backs revealed truth with all the energy of God and fills it through and through. Unction is simply God put into His own word and onto His own preachers. Through mighty and great prayerfulness, and through continual prayerfulness, it becomes fully potent and personal to the preacher. It inspires and clarifies his mind and gives him insight, grasp and power to drive the truth home. It gives the preacher heart power, which is greater than head power; and through it tenderness, purity and force flow from the heart. Enlargement, freedom, fullness of thought, and directness and simplicity of speech are the fruits of this unction.

Earnestness is often mistaken for this unction. The one who has the divine unction will be earnest, by the very spiritual nature of things; but there may be a great deal of earnestness without the slightest trace of unction.

From some points of view, earnestness and unction look alike. Earnestness can easily, and without anyone noticing, be substituted for unction or mistaken for it. It takes a spiritual eye and a spiritual taste to tell them apart.

Earnestness may be sincere, serious, ardent and persevering. It takes up a thing with good will, pursues it with perseverance and urges it with ardor; it puts force into it. But none of these forces rises higher than the merely human. The man is in it — the whole man, with all he has of will and heart, of brain and genius, of planning and working and talking. He has set himself to some purpose that has mastered him, and he pursues it in order to master it. There may be nothing of God in it. There may be little of God in it, precisely because there is so much of the man in it. He may put forward arguments for his earnest purpose that please, or touch and move, or overwhelm people with a conviction of their importance; and in all this, earnestness may travel along earthly roads, driven by human forces alone, its altar built by earthly hands and its fire lit by earthly flames. It is said of a rather famous and gifted preacher, who interpreted Scripture to suit his fancy or his purpose, that he “grew very eloquent over his own exegesis.” In the same way men grow extremely earnest over their own plans or movements. Earnestness may be selfishness in disguise.

What about unction? It is the indefinable thing in preaching that makes it preaching. It is what distinguishes and separates preaching from all merely human speeches. It is the divine in preaching. It makes the preaching sharp to those who need sharpness. It falls like the dew on those who need to be refreshed. It is well described as:

“a two-edged sword

Of heavenly temper keen,

And double were the wounds it made

Wherever it glanced between.

’Twas death to sin; ’twas life

To all who mourned for sin.

It kindled and it silenced strife,

Made war and peace within.”

This unction comes to the preacher not in the study but in the prayer closet. It is heaven’s distillation in answer to prayer. It is the sweetest breath of the Holy Spirit. It saturates, fills, softens, seeps through, cuts and soothes. It carries the Word like dynamite, like salt, like sugar. It makes the Word a comforter, an arranger, a revealer, a searcher. It makes the hearer either a guilty man or a saint; it makes him weep like a child and live like a giant; it opens his heart and his purse as gently, yet as strongly, as the spring opens the leaves. This unction is not the gift of genius. It is not found in the halls of learning. No eloquence can coax it. No hard work can earn it. No bishop’s hands can confer it. It is the gift of God — the seal He sets on His own messengers. It is heaven’s knighthood, given to the chosen, true and brave ones who have sought this anointed honor through many hours of tearful, wrestling prayer.

Earnestness is good and impressive; genius is gifted and great. Thought kindles and inspires. But it takes a more divine endowment, a more powerful energy than earnestness or genius or thought, to break the chains of sin, to win estranged and depraved hearts to God, to repair the breaches and to restore the Church to her old ways of purity and power. Nothing but this holy unction can do this.

No one can describe what it is or where it comes from, but with a sweet violence it pierces into the heart and the affections, and it comes directly from the Word. And if there is any way to obtain such a thing, it is through the heavenly disposition of the speaker.” We call it unction. It is this unction that makes the word of God “quick and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” It is this unction that gives the preacher’s words such point, sharpness and power, and that creates such friction and stir in many a dead congregation. The same truths have been told strictly according to the letter, as smooth as human oil could make them — but with no signs of life, not a single pulse beat; everything as peaceful as the grave, and as dead. Then the same preacher receives a baptism of this unction. The divine breath is on him; the letter of the Word has been adorned and set on fire by this mysterious power; and the throbbings of life begin — life that receives, or life that resists. The unction pervades the conscience and convicts it, and it breaks the heart. This divine unction is the feature that separates and distinguishes true gospel preaching from every other way of presenting the truth, and it creates a wide spiritual gulf between the preacher who has it and the one who does not. It backs revealed truth with all the energy of God and fills it through and through. Unction is simply God put into His own word and onto His own preachers. Through mighty and great prayerfulness, and through continual prayerfulness, it becomes fully potent and personal to the preacher. It inspires and clarifies his mind and gives him insight, grasp and power to drive the truth home. It gives the preacher heart power, which is greater than head power; and through it tenderness, purity and force flow from the heart. Enlargement, freedom, fullness of thought, and directness and simplicity of speech are the fruits of this unction. Earnestness is often mistaken for this unction. The one who has the divine unction will be earnest, by the very spiritual nature of things; but there may be a great deal of earnestness without the slightest trace of unction. From some points of view, earnestness and unction look alike. Earnestness can easily, and without anyone noticing, be substituted for unction or mistaken for it. It takes a spiritual eye and a spiritual taste to tell them apart. Earnestness may be sincere, serious, ardent and persevering. It takes up a thing with good will, pursues it with perseverance and urges it with ardor; it puts force into it. But none of these forces rises higher than the merely human. The man is in it — the whole man, with all he has of will and heart, of brain and genius, of planning and working and talking. He has set himself to some purpose that has mastered him, and he pursues it in order to master it. There may be nothing of God in it. There may be little of God in it, precisely because there is so much of the man in it. He may put forward arguments for his earnest purpose that please, or touch and move, or overwhelm people with a conviction of their importance; and in all this, earnestness may travel along earthly roads, driven by human forces alone, its altar built by earthly hands and its fire lit by earthly flames. It is said of a rather famous and gifted preacher, who interpreted Scripture to suit his fancy or his purpose, that he “grew very eloquent over his own exegesis.” In the same way men grow extremely earnest over their own plans or movements. Earnestness may be selfishness in disguise. What about unction? It is the indefinable thing in preaching that makes it preaching. It is what distinguishes and separates preaching from all merely human speeches. It is the divine in preaching. It makes the preaching sharp to those who need sharpness. It falls like the dew on those who need to be refreshed. It is well described as: “a two-edged sword Of heavenly temper keen, And double were the wounds it made Wherever it glanced between. ’Twas death to sin; ’twas life To all who mourned for sin. It kindled and it silenced strife, Made war and peace within.” This unction comes to the preacher not in the study but in the prayer closet. It is heaven’s distillation in answer to prayer. It is the sweetest breath of the Holy Spirit. It saturates, fills, softens, seeps through, cuts and soothes. It carries the Word like dynamite, like salt, like sugar. It makes the Word a comforter, an arranger, a revealer, a searcher. It makes the hearer either a guilty man or a saint; it makes him weep like a child and live like a giant; it opens his heart and his purse as gently, yet as strongly, as the spring opens the leaves. This unction is not the gift of genius. It is not found in the halls of learning. No eloquence can coax it. No hard work can earn it. No bishop’s hands can confer it. It is the gift of God — the seal He sets on His own messengers. It is heaven’s knighthood, given to the chosen, true and brave ones who have sought this anointed honor through many hours of tearful, wrestling prayer. Earnestness is good and impressive; genius is gifted and great. Thought kindles and inspires. But it takes a more divine endowment, a more powerful energy than earnestness or genius or thought, to break the chains of sin, to win estranged and depraved hearts to God, to repair the breaches and to restore the Church to her old ways of purity and power. Nothing but this holy unction can do this.

fields.title: Much Prayer the Price of Unction
fields.body_html:
All the minister’s efforts will be vanity, or worse than vanity, if he does not have unction. Unction must come down from heaven and spread a savor and feeling and relish over his ministry. Among the other means of fitting himself for his office, the Bible must hold the first place, and the last place too must be given to the Word of God and prayer.—Richard Cecil

In the Christian system, unction is the anointing of the Holy Ghost, which sets a person apart for God’s work and equips them for it. This unction is the one divine enabling by which the preacher achieves the distinctive and saving purposes of preaching. Without this unction no true spiritual results are achieved; the results and forces of the preaching rise no higher than the results of unsanctified speech. Without unction, such speech is as powerful as the pulpit.

This divine unction on the preacher produces, through the Word of God, the spiritual results that flow from the gospel; and without this unction those results are not obtained. Many pleasant impressions may be made, but they all fall far short of the purposes of gospel preaching. This unction can be imitated. There are many things that look like it, and many results that resemble its effects; but they are foreign both to its results and to its nature. The fervor or tenderness stirred up by a moving or emotional sermon may look like the workings of the divine unction, but they have no sharp, penetrating, heart-breaking force. There is no heart-healing balm in these surface-level, sympathetic, emotional stirrings. They do not go to the root; they neither search out sin nor cure it.

This divine unction is the one distinguishing feature that separates true gospel preaching from every other way of presenting truth. It backs the revealed truth with all the force of God and fills it through and through. It sheds light on the Word, broadens and enriches the mind, and empowers it to grasp and understand the Word. It equips the preacher’s heart and brings it into that condition of tenderness, purity, force and light that is necessary to obtain the highest results. This unction gives the preacher liberty and enlargement of thought and soul — a freedom, fullness and directness of speech that no other process can provide.

Without this unction on the preacher, the gospel has no more power to spread itself than any other system of truth. This is the seal of its divinity. Unction in the preacher puts God in the gospel. Without the unction God is absent, and the gospel is left to the low and unsatisfying forces that human ingenuity, interest or talent can devise to press its doctrines home and carry them forward.

It is in this element, more than in any other, that the pulpit fails. It falls short at exactly this all-important point. It may have learning; brilliance and eloquence may delight and charm; sensational methods, or less offensive ones, may bring the public in crowds; mental power may impress the truth and drive it home with all its resources; but without this unction, each and every one of these will be no more than the restless assault of the waves on a Gibraltar. Spray and foam may cover the rock and make it sparkle; but the rocks are still there, unmoved and unmovable. These human forces can no more sweep the hardness and sin out of the human heart than the ocean’s ceaseless flow can sweep those rocks away.

This unction is the force of consecration, and its presence is the continuing test of that consecration. It is this divine anointing on the preacher that secures his consecration to God and to his work. Other forces and motives may call him to the work, but this alone is consecration. Being set apart for God’s work by the power of the Holy Spirit is the only consecration God recognizes as legitimate.

The unction — the divine unction, this heavenly anointing — is what the pulpit needs and must have. This divine and heavenly oil, put on it by the laying on of God’s hand, must soften and oil the whole man — heart, head and spirit — until it separates him with a mighty separation from all earthly, secular, worldly and selfish motives and aims, and sets him apart foreverything that is pure and Godlike.

It is the presence of this unction on the preacher that creates the stir and friction in many a congregation. The same truths have been told strictly according to the letter, but not a ripple has been seen, not a pain or a pulse felt. Everything is as quiet as a graveyard. Then another preacher comes, and this mysterious influence is on him. The letter of the Word has been set on fire by the Spirit, and the upheavals of a mighty movement are felt. It is the unction that pervades and stirs the conscience and breaks the heart. Preaching without unction makes everything hard, dry, bitter and dead.

This unction is not just a memory or something from a past era; it is a present, realized, conscious fact. It belongs to the man’s experience as well as to his preaching. It is what transforms him into the image of his divine Master, as well as what enables him to declare the truths of Christ with power. It is so truly the power in the ministry that without it everything else seems feeble and empty, and its presence makes up for the absence of every other, feebler force.

This unction is not a gift that can never be lost. It is a conditional gift, and its presence is kept up and increased by the same process by which it was first obtained: by unceasing prayer to God, by passionate longings for God, by valuing it, by seeking it with tireless ardor, and by counting everything else loss and failure without it.

How does this unction come, and where from? Directly from God in answer to prayer. Only praying hearts are filled with this holy oil; only praying lips are anointed with this divine unction.

Prayer, much prayer, is the price of unction in preaching; prayer, much prayer, is the one and only condition of keeping this unction. Without unceasing prayer the unction never comes to the preacher. Without perseverance in prayer the unction, like manna kept overnight, breeds worms.

fields.title: Prayer Marks Spiritual Leadership
fields.body_html:
Give me one hundred preachers who fear nothing but sin and desire nothing but God, and I do not care a straw whether they are clergymen or laymen; such men alone will shake the gates of hell and set up the kingdom of heaven on earth. God does nothing except in answer to prayer.—John Wesley

The apostles knew how necessary and how valuable prayer was to their ministry. They knew that their high commission as apostles, far from releasing them from the need to pray, bound them to it by an even more urgent need. So they were intensely watchful in case some other important work should use up their time and keep them from praying as they ought. That is why they appointed laymen to take care of the delicate and absorbing duties of serving the poor, so that they, the apostles, might without hindrance “give themselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” Prayer is put first, and their relationship to prayer is stated in the strongest terms — “give themselves to it”: making a business of it, surrendering themselves to praying, and putting fervor, urgency, perseverance and time into it.

How these holy, apostolic men devoted themselves to this divine work of prayer! “Night and day praying exceedingly,” says Paul. “We will give ourselves continually to prayer” is the united voice of apostolic devotion. How these New Testament preachers poured themselves out in prayer for God’s people! How they brought God in full force into their Churches by their praying! These holy apostles did not foolishly imagine that they had fulfilled their high and solemn duties simply by faithfully delivering God’s word. Their preaching was made to stick and to tell by the ardor and insistence of their praying. Apostolic praying was as demanding, toilsome and urgent as apostolic preaching. They prayed mightily day and night to bring their people to the highest regions of faith and holiness. They prayed more mightily still to keep them at that high spiritual altitude. The preacher who has never learned, in the school of Christ, the high and divine art of interceding for his people will never learn the art of preaching — though homiletics be poured into him by the ton, and though he be the most gifted genius at making and delivering sermons.

The prayers of apostolic, saintly leaders do much to make saints of those who are not apostles. If the Church leaders of later years had been as careful and fervent in praying for their people as the apostles were, the sad, dark times of worldliness and apostasy would not have spoiled the Church’s history, eclipsed its glory and halted its advance. Apostolic praying makes apostolic saints and keeps apostolic times of purity and power in the Church.

What loftiness of soul, what purity and nobility of motive, what unselfishness, what self-sacrifice, what exhausting toil, what ardor of spirit, what divine tact it takes to be an intercessor for others!

The preacher is to pour himself out in prayer for his people — not simply that they might be saved, but that they might be mightily saved. The apostles poured themselves out in prayer that their saints might be perfect; not that they should have a little taste for the things of God, but that they “might be filled with all the fullness of God.” Paul did not rely on his apostolic preaching to achieve this; rather, “for this cause he bowed his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Paul’s praying carried Paul’s converts farther along the highway of sainthood than Paul’s preaching did. Epaphras did as much for the Colossian saints by prayer as by his preaching, or more. He labored fervently in prayer for them always, that “they might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.”

Preachers are, above all, God’s leaders. They bear the primary responsibility for the condition of the Church. They shape its character and give tone and direction to its life.

A great deal, in every way, depends on these leaders. They shape the times and the institutions. The Church is divine, and the treasure it holds is heavenly, but it bears the stamp of the human. The treasure is in earthen vessels, and it tastes of the vessel. The Church of God makes its leaders or is made by them. Either way, it will be what its leaders are: spiritual if they are spiritual, worldly if they are worldly, a mixture if its leaders are a mixture. Israel’s kings set the character of Israel’s godliness. A Church rarely rebels against the religion of its leaders or rises above it. Strongly spiritual leaders — men of holy might at the head — are signs of God’s favor; disaster and weakness follow in the wake of feeble or worldly leaders. Israel had sunk low when God gave children to be their princes and babes to rule over them. The prophets predict no happy state when children oppress God’s Israel and women rule over them. Times of spiritual leadership are times of great spiritual prosperity for the Church.

Prayer is one of the outstanding marks of strong spiritual leadership. Men of mighty prayer are men of might, and they shape things. Their power with God has the tread of a conqueror.

How can a man preach who does not get his message fresh from God in the prayer closet? How can he preach without having his faith quickened, his vision cleared and his heart warmed by his time shut away with God? Alas for the pulpit lips that this flame from the prayer closet has never touched! They will always be dry and without unction, and divine truths will never come with power from lips like these. As far as the real interests of religion are concerned, a pulpit without a prayer closet will always be a barren thing.

A preacher may preach without prayer in an official, entertaining or learned way; but between that kind of preaching and sowing God’s precious seed with holy hands and prayerful, weeping hearts there is an immeasurable distance.

A prayerless ministry is the undertaker for all God’s truth and for God’s Church. He may have the most expensive casket and the most beautiful flowers, but it is a funeral all the same, for all the charming display. A prayerless Christian will never learn God’s truth; a prayerless ministry will never be able to teach God’s truth. Ages of millennial glory have been lost by a prayerless Church. The coming of our Lord has been postponed indefinitely by a prayerless Church. Hell has enlarged herself and filled her dreadful caves while a prayerless Church went through its dead service.

The best and greatest offering is an offering of prayer. If the preachers of the twentieth century will learn the lesson of prayer well, and use the power of prayer fully, the millennium will reach its noon before the century ends. “Pray without ceasing” is the trumpet call to the preachers of the twentieth century. If the preachers of the twentieth century will get their texts, their thoughts, their words and their sermons in their prayer closets, the next century will find a new heaven and a new earth. The old heaven and earth, stained and darkened by sin, will pass away under the power of a praying ministry.

fields.title: Preachers Need the Prayers of the People
fields.body_html:
If some Christians who have been complaining about their ministers had said and done less before people, and had applied themselves with all their might to crying out to God for their ministers — had, so to speak, risen up and stormed heaven with humble, fervent and unceasing prayers for them — they would have been much more likely to succeed.—Jonathan Edwards

Somehow the practice of praying specifically for the preacher has fallen out of use or come to be undervalued. Now and then we have heard the practice attacked as a slight on the ministry, as though those who do it were publicly declaring that the ministry is inadequate. Perhaps it offends the pride of learning and self-sufficiency — and these ought to be offended and rebuked in a ministry that is negligent enough to let them exist.

To the preacher, prayer is not simply a duty of his profession, or a privilege; it is a necessity. Air is no more necessary to the lungs than prayer is to the preacher. It is absolutely necessary for the preacher to pray. It is an absolute necessity that the preacher be prayed for. These two statements are joined in a marriage that should never know divorce: the preacher must pray; the preacher must be prayed for. It will take all the praying he can do, and all the praying he can get others to do, to meet his fearful responsibilities and to gain the greatest and truest success in his great work. The true preacher, next to cultivating the spirit and the practice of prayer in himself in their most intense form, longs with a great longing for the prayers of God’s people.

The holier a person is, the more they value prayer, and the more clearly they see that God gives Himself to those who pray, and that the measure of God’s revelation to the soul is the measure of the soul’s longing, persistent prayer for God. Salvation never finds its way into a prayerless heart. The Holy Spirit never dwells in a prayerless spirit. Preaching never builds up a prayerless soul. Christ knows nothing of prayerless Christians. The gospel cannot be carried forward by a prayerless preacher. Gifts, talents, education, eloquence and God’s call cannot lessen the demand for prayer; they only intensify the need for the preacher to pray and to be prayed for. The more the preacher’s eyes are opened to the nature, the responsibility and the difficulties of his work, the more he will see — and, if he is a true preacher, the more he will feel — the need for prayer: not only the growing demand to pray himself, but to call on others to help him by their prayers.

Paul is an example of this. Single prayers combined, like drops of water, make an ocean that nothing can resist. fields.title: Deliberation Necessary to Largest Results from Prayer
fields.body_html:
This constant rush of business and company is ruining me in soul, if not in body. More solitude and earlier hours! I suspect I have habitually been giving too little time to religious exercises such as private devotion, religious meditation, Scripture reading and so on. That is why I am lean and cold and hard. I had better set aside two hours, or an hour and a half, every day. I have been keeping hours that are too late, and so have had only a hurried half hour to myself in the morning. Surely the experience of all good men confirms that without a proper measure of private devotion the soul will grow lean. But everything can be done through prayer — almighty prayer, I am ready to say — and why not? For it is almighty only through the gracious appointment of the God of love and truth. Oh, then, pray, pray, pray!—William Wilberforce

Our devotions are not measured by the clock, but time is of their essence. The ability to wait and stay and press on belongs essentially to our communion with God. Hurry, which is unbecoming and damaging everywhere, is alarmingly so in the great business of communion with God. Short devotions are the ruin of deep godliness. Calmness, grasp and strength never keep company with hurry. Short devotions drain spiritual vigor, halt spiritual progress, undermine spiritual foundations, and blight both the root and the bloom of spiritual life. They are the fertile source of backsliding and the sure sign of a superficial godliness. They deceive, they blight, they rot the seed and they impoverish the soil.

It is true that the prayers of the Bible, as written and printed, are short; but the praying men of the Bible were with God through many sweet and holy hours of wrestling. They won by few words but long waiting. The prayers Moses records may be short, but Moses prayed to God with fasting and mighty crying for forty days and nights.

The account of Elijah’s praying can be condensed into a few brief paragraphs; but no doubt Elijah, who when “praying he prayed,” spent many hours of fiery struggle and lofty communion with God before he could say to Ahab with confident boldness, “There shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.” The written summary of Paul’s prayers is short, but Paul “prayed night and day exceedingly.” The “Lord’s Prayer” is a divine summary for the lips of infants, but the man Christ Jesus prayed through many a whole night before His work was done; and His all-night and long-sustained devotions gave His work its finish and perfection, and gave His character the fullness and glory of its divinity.

Spiritual work is demanding work, and people are reluctant to do it. Praying — true praying — costs an outlay of serious attention and of time, which flesh and blood do not enjoy. Few people are made of fiber strong enough to make a costly outlay when surface work will pass just as well in the market. We can get so used to our beggarly praying that it looks fine to us; at least it keeps up a decent appearance and quiets the conscience — the deadliest of drugs! We can neglect our praying and not realize the danger until the foundations are gone. Hurried devotions make for weak faith, feeble convictions and questionable godliness. To be little with God is to be little for God. Cutting short our praying makes our whole religious character short, skimpy, stingy and slovenly.

It takes plenty of time for God to flow fully into the spirit. Short devotions cut the pipe through which God flows in fullness. It takes time in the secret places to receive the full revelation of God. Too little time and too much hurry spoil the picture.

Henry Martyn laments that “lack of private devotional reading, and shortness of prayer because of incessant sermon-making, had produced much distance between God and his soul.” He judged that he had given too much time to public ministry and too little to private communion with God. He was strongly moved to set apart times for fasting and to devote times to solemn prayer. As a result he records: “Was helped this morning to pray for two hours.” William Wilberforce, the equal of kings, said: “I must make sure of more time for private devotions. I have been living far too publicly for my own good. Cutting short private devotions starves the soul; it grows lean and faint. I have been keeping hours that are too late.” Of a failure in Parliament he says: “Let me record my grief and shame — and all of it, probably, from private devotions having been cut short, and so God let me stumble.” More solitude and earlier hours was his remedy.

More time and early hours for prayer would work like magic to revive and strengthen many a decayed spiritual life. More time and early hours for prayer would show themselves in holy living. A holy life would not be such a rare or difficult thing if our devotions were not so short and hurried. A Christlike temper, with its sweet and calm fragrance, would not be so foreign and hopeless an inheritance if our time in the prayer closet were lengthened and deepened. We live shabbily because we pray poorly. Plenty of time to feast in our prayer closets will bring marrow and fatness to our lives. Our ability to stay with God in the prayer closet measures our ability to stay with God outside it. Hasty visits to the prayer closet are deceptive and leave us short. Not only are we fooled by them, but we lose by them in many ways and miss many rich inheritances. Lingering in the prayer closet teaches and wins. We are taught by it, and the greatest victories are often the result of great waiting — waiting until words and plans are used up, and silent, patient waiting wins the crown. Jesus Christ asks with indignant emphasis, “Shall not God avenge his own elect which cry day and night unto him?”

To pray is the greatest thing we can do; and to do it well there must be calmness, time and deliberation. Otherwise it is reduced to the smallest and meanest of things. True praying has the greatest results for good, and poor praying the least. We cannot do too much real praying; we cannot do too little of the sham kind. We must learn the worth of prayer all over again and enter the school of prayer all over again. There is nothing that takes more time to learn. And if we want to learn this wonderful art, we must not give it a scrap of time here and there — “A little talk with Jesus,” as the tiny little saints sing — but we must demand the best hours of the day for God and prayer and hold on to them with an iron grip, or there will be no praying worthy of the name.

This, however, is not a day of prayer. There are few people who pray. Prayer is run down by preacher and priest. In these days of hurry and bustle, of electricity and steam, people will not take time to pray. There are preachers who “say prayers” as part of their program, on regular or formal occasions; but who “stirs himself up to take hold upon God?” Who prays as Jacob prayed — until he is crowned as a prevailing, princely intercessor? Who prays as Elijah prayed — until all the locked-up forces of nature were unsealed and a famine-stricken land bloomed like the garden of God? Who prays as Jesus Christ prayed when, out on the mountain, He “continued all night in prayer to God?” The apostles “gave themselves to prayer” — the hardest thing to get people, or even preachers, to do. There are laymen who will give their money — some of them in rich abundance — but they will not “give themselves” to prayer, and without it their money is nothing but a curse. There are plenty of preachers who will preach and give great and eloquent addresses on the need for revival and the spread of the kingdom of God, but there are not many who will do the one thing without which all preaching and organizing are worse than useless — pray. It is out of date, almost a lost art; and the greatest benefactor this age could have is the man who will bring the preachers and the Church back to prayer.

fields.title: A Praying Pulpit Begets a Praying Pew
fields.body_html:
I consider that my prayer is more than a match for the devil himself; if it were otherwise, Luther would have fared very differently long before now. Yet people will not see and acknowledge the great wonders or miracles God works on my behalf. If I were to neglect prayer for even a single day, I would lose a great deal of the fire of faith.—Martin Luther

Before Pentecost the apostles could get only glimpses of the great importance of prayer. But when the Spirit came and filled them at Pentecost, He raised prayer to its vital and all-commanding place in the gospel of Christ. Today the call of prayer to every saint is the Spirit’s loudest and most urgent call. The godliness of the saints is made, refined and perfected by prayer. The gospel moves at a slow and timid pace when the saints are not at their prayers early and late and long.

Where are the Christlike leaders who can teach today’s saints how to pray and set them to it? Do we realize that we are raising up a prayerless generation of saints? Where are the apostolic leaders who can set God’s people praying? Let them come to the front and do the work, and it will be the greatest work that can be done. More educational resources and a great increase in financial power will be the worst curse to religion if they are not sanctified by more and better praying than we are doing. More praying will not come automatically. The campaign for the twentieth- or thirtieth-century fund will not help our praying but hinder it, if we are not careful. Nothing but a deliberate effort by a praying leadership will do. Those at the head must lead the apostolic effort to root the vital importance and the fact of prayer in the heart and life of the Church. Only praying leaders can have praying followers. Praying apostles will produce praying saints. A praying pulpit will produce praying pews. We greatly need someone who can set the saints to this business of praying. We are not a generation of praying saints. Non-praying saints are a beggarly gang of saints, with neither the ardor nor the beauty nor the power of saints. Who will repair this breach? Whoever can set the Church praying will be the greatest of reformers and apostles.

It is our most sober judgment that the great need of the Church, in this and every age, is men of such commanding faith, such spotless holiness, such marked spiritual vigor and consuming zeal, that their prayers, faith, lives and ministry will be of such a radical and aggressive kind as to bring about spiritual revolutions that mark new eras in the lives of individuals and of the Church.

We do not mean men who stir up sensations with novel gimmicks, or those who draw people with pleasing entertainment. We mean men who can stir things and work revolutions by preaching God’s Word and by the power of the Holy Ghost — revolutions that change the whole current of things.

Natural ability and educational advantages are not factors in this matter. What counts is capacity for faith, the ability to pray, the power of thorough consecration, the ability to make oneself small, a complete losing of oneself in God’s glory, and an ever-present, insatiable yearning and seeking after all the fullness of God — men who can set the Church ablaze for God; not in a noisy, showy way, but with an intense and quiet heat that melts and moves everything for God.

God can work wonders if He can get a suitable man. Men can work wonders if they can get God to lead them. The full endowment of the Spirit that turned the world upside down would be supremely useful in these latter days. Men who can stir things mightily for God, whose spiritual revolutions change the whole face of things, are the universal need of the Church.

The Church has never been without such men. They adorn its history; they are the standing miracles that prove the Church is divine; their example and their story are an unfailing inspiration and blessing. Our prayer should be for an increase in their number and power.

What has been done in spiritual matters can be done again, and done better. This was Christ’s view. He said, “Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father.” The past has not used up either the possibilities or the demands for doing great things for God. The Church that depends on its past history for its miracles of power and grace is a fallen Church.

God wants chosen men — men from whom self and the world have been driven out by a severe crucifixion, by a bankruptcy that has so totally ruined self and the world that there is neither hope nor desire of recovery; men who, through this bankruptcy and crucifixion, have turned perfect hearts toward God.

Let us pray ardently that God’s promise to prayer may be more than fulfilled.

Where are the apostolic leaders who can set God’s people praying? Let them come to the front and do the work, and it will be the greatest work that can be done. More educational resources and a great increase in financial power will be the worst curse to religion if they are not sanctified by more and better praying than we are doing. More praying will not come automatically. The campaign for the twentieth- or thirtieth-century fund will not help our praying but hinder it, if we are not careful. Nothing but a deliberate effort by a praying leadership will do. Those at the head must lead the apostolic effort to root the vital importance and the fact of prayer in the heart and life of the Church. Only praying leaders can have praying followers. Praying apostles will produce praying saints. A praying pulpit will produce praying pews. We greatly need someone who can set the saints to this business of praying. We are not a generation of praying saints. Non-praying saints are a beggarly gang of saints, with neither the ardor nor the beauty nor the power of saints. Who will repair this breach? Whoever can set the Church praying will be the greatest of reformers and apostles. It is our most sober judgment that the great need of the Church, in this and every age, is men of such commanding faith, such spotless holiness, such marked spiritual vigor and consuming zeal, that their prayers, faith, lives and ministry will be of such a radical and aggressive kind as to bring about spiritual revolutions that mark new eras in the lives of individuals and of the Church. We do not mean men who stir up sensations with novel gimmicks, or those who draw people with pleasing entertainment. We mean men who can stir things and work revolutions by preaching God’s Word and by the power of the Holy Ghost — revolutions that change the whole current of things. Natural ability and educational advantages are not factors in this matter. What counts is capacity for faith, the ability to pray, the power of thorough consecration, the ability to make oneself small, a complete losing of oneself in God’s glory, and an ever-present, insatiable yearning and seeking after all the fullness of God — men who can set the Church ablaze for God; not in a noisy, showy way, but with an intense and quiet heat that melts and moves everything for God. God can work wonders if He can get a suitable man. Men can work wonders if they can get God to lead them. The full endowment of the Spirit that turned the world upside down would be supremely useful in these latter days. Men who can stir things mightily for God, whose spiritual revolutions change the whole face of things, are the universal need of the Church. The Church has never been without such men. They adorn its history; they are the standing miracles that prove the Church is divine; their example and their story are an unfailing inspiration and blessing. Our prayer should be for an increase in their number and power. What has been done in spiritual matters can be done again, and done better. This was Christ’s view. He said, “Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also; and greater works than these shall he do; because I go unto my Father.” The past has not used up either the possibilities or the demands for doing great things for God. The Church that depends on its past history for its miracles of power and grace is a fallen Church. God wants chosen men — men from whom self and the world have been driven out by a severe crucifixion, by a bankruptcy that has so totally ruined self and the world that there is neither hope nor desire of recovery; men who, through this bankruptcy and crucifixion, have turned perfect hearts toward God. Let us pray ardently that God’s promise to prayer may be more than fulfilled.
